name: Three-Act Structure
one_line_summary: Setup, confrontation, resolution — dominant Western dramatic structure.
extended_summary: The Three-Act Structure is the dominant Western dramatic framework dividing narrative into three principal sections: Act I (Setup) introducing characters, world, and central conflict, typically ending with an inciting incident or first plot point that propels the protagonist into the main story; Act II (Confrontation) developing the central conflict through rising complications, typically the longest act, often with a midpoint reversal and second plot point that drives toward climax; Act III (Resolution) bringing conflict to climactic confrontation and resolving narrative threads. The framework substantially descends from Aristotle's Poetics (4th century BCE) emphasizing beginning, middle, and end as essential narrative components, with subsequent development through Roman and medieval dramatic theory and substantial codification through 20th-century Hollywood screenwriting tradition. The framework was substantially popularized for contemporary screenwriting through Syd Field's 1979 Screenplay: The Foundations of Screenwriting, which articulated specific page-count proportions for a 120-page screenplay (roughly 30/60/30 pages for the three acts) and named specific structural beats (Plot Point 1 around page 25-30 launching Act II, Midpoint around page 60, Plot Point 2 around page 85-90 launching Act III). Field's substantial influence shaped subsequent Hollywood practice and screenwriting education. The framework has been substantially extended through additional structural frameworks (Save the Cat Beat Sheet, separately enriched, providing finer-grained beat structure within three-act framework). Critics including substantial scholars argue: three-act structure reflects particular Western (especially Hollywood) dramatic conventions rather than universal narrative form; many successful narratives don't fit cleanly into three acts (episodic structure, ensemble narrative, non-Western dramatic traditions); the rigid page-count proportions Field articulated produce formulaic screenplays; alternative structural frameworks (four-act, five-act, eight-sequence) provide useful alternatives.

name: Five-Act Structure
one_line_summary: Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, denouement.
extended_summary: The Five-Act Structure (Freytag's Pyramid) is the dramatic framework articulated by German novelist and playwright Gustav Freytag in his 1863 Die Technik des Dramas (translated as Technique of the Drama 1894), substantially analyzing classical Greek tragedy and Shakespearean drama into five-act structure with characteristic pyramid shape: (1) Exposition (introduction of characters, setting, situation); (2) Rising Action (complications and obstacles building toward central crisis); (3) Climax (decisive turning point of the action); (4) Falling Action (consequences flowing from climax, with subordinate complications); (5) Denouement or Catastrophe (final resolution, often catastrophic in tragedy). Freytag's analysis substantially codified what classical and Renaissance dramatic theory had developed less systematically. The five-act structure descends from classical Greek and Roman dramatic tradition (Horace's three-or-five-act recommendation in Ars Poetica c. 19 BCE) and substantial Renaissance and neoclassical practice, with Shakespeare's plays substantially providing exemplary five-act exemplars (most printed Shakespeare editions impose five-act divisions, though Shakespeare's original folios show varied act divisions and many scholars argue Shakespeare composed continuously rather than in five distinct acts). Freytag's Pyramid is foundational to literary education and dramatic analysis, particularly in classical literary analysis and traditional theater studies. Contemporary screenwriting has substantially superseded five-act structure with three-act structure (separately enriched) for commercial film, though five-act structure remains substantially relevant for: classical and Shakespearean drama education; long-form television (where the act-break structure aligns with commercial breaks in network television, though streaming has substantially complicated this); some novel structures particularly literary fiction. Critics note: Freytag's Pyramid as taught is somewhat schematic — actual successful drama rarely fits the rigid pyramid shape; the framework reflects particular German-Romantic interpretation of Greek tragedy that subsequent classical scholarship has substantially refined; non-Western dramatic traditions don't fit the framework cleanly.

name: Save the Cat Beat Sheet
one_line_summary: Snyder's fifteen-beat screenplay structure widely used in Hollywood.
extended_summary: The Save the Cat Beat Sheet is the fifteen-beat screenplay structural framework articulated by Hollywood screenwriter Blake Snyder in his 2005 Save the Cat! The Last Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need (with subsequent Save the Cat Goes to the Movies 2007 and Save the Cat Strikes Back 2009). Snyder's framework operationalized three-act structure (separately enriched) into specific beats with target page numbers in a standard 110-page screenplay: (1) Opening Image (page 1, sets tone); (2) Theme Stated (page 5); (3) Setup (pages 1-10, introduces protagonist's world); (4) Catalyst (page 12, inciting incident); (5) Debate (pages 12-25, protagonist's reluctance); (6) Break Into Two (page 25, commitment to journey); (7) B Story (page 30, secondary plot, often love interest); (8) Fun and Games (pages 30-55, 'promise of the premise' delivers genre expectations); (9) Midpoint (page 55, false victory or false defeat); (10) Bad Guys Close In (pages 55-75); (11) All Is Lost (page 75, lowest point); (12) Dark Night of the Soul (pages 75-85); (13) Break Into Three (page 85, solution emerges); (14) Finale (pages 85-110, climactic action); (15) Final Image (page 110, mirror of opening). The 'save the cat' title refers to Snyder's principle of giving the protagonist a likeable early action (literally saving a cat) to win audience sympathy. The framework has been enormously influential in Hollywood screenwriting from the mid-2000s onward — substantial proportion of contemporary mainstream films can be analyzed through Snyder's beats, with substantial commercial training and software (Save the Cat software, online courses, certification programs) building on Snyder's methodology. The framework has also drawn substantial criticism for producing formulaic mainstream films — substantial Hollywood discourse blames 'Save the Cat formula' for the perceived sameness of contemporary mainstream cinema, with substantial published criticism arguing Snyder's beats homogenize creative work that should be distinctive.

name: Story Circle
one_line_summary: Harmon's eight-step distillation of Campbell's monomyth for episodic storytelling.
extended_summary: The Story Circle is the eight-step narrative framework articulated by television writer and showrunner Dan Harmon (creator of Community, co-creator of Rick and Morty) as practical distillation of Joseph Campbell's monomyth (Hero with a Thousand Faces 1949) for episodic television storytelling. Harmon's eight steps form a circular structure: (1) A character is in a zone of comfort; (2) But they want something; (3) They enter an unfamiliar situation; (4) Adapt to it; (5) Get what they wanted; (6) Pay a heavy price for it; (7) Then return to their familiar situation; (8) Having changed. The framework's circular structure emphasizes that the protagonist returns to a similar situation but with substantial transformation — a 'descent and return' pattern that descends from Campbell's monomyth (departure, initiation, return) but is operationalized for the substantial constraints of episodic television (where each episode typically returns characters to the situation that enables the series to continue). Harmon developed the framework substantially through his work on television (substantial Channel 101 short-film community in early 2000s, then his television production), with the framework substantially circulated through online writing about his methodology and through interviews. The Story Circle has been substantially adopted by writers in television, comics, novels, and games — providing accessible practical framework for narrative development that's substantially less rigid than Campbell's elaborate seventeen-stage monomyth or Vogler's Writer's Journey adaptation (separately enriched). The framework's commercial success has been substantial in the streaming-television era, with substantial influence on showrunner methodology. Critics note the framework's substantial debt to Campbell brings forward Campbell's substantial issues — substantially Western androcentric framing, substantial overgeneralization of 'universal' narrative pattern, substantial assumptions about character transformation that don't apply to all stories. Some narrative theorists argue the framework's universality claims overstate what episodic television demonstrates.

name: Pixar Story Spine
one_line_summary: Once upon a time / every day / one day / because of that / until finally / and ever since then.
extended_summary: The Pixar Story Spine is the narrative-development framework using a fill-in-the-blank sentence structure: 'Once upon a time _____. Every day, _____. One day _____. Because of that, _____. Because of that, _____. Until finally _____. And ever since then, _____.' The framework was substantially developed by improv theater pioneer Kenn Adams in the 1990s for improv-based storytelling exercises and was substantially popularized through Pixar story-development practice — particularly through former Pixar story artist Emma Coats's 2011-2012 'Pixar's 22 Rules of Storytelling' Twitter thread, where the Story Spine appeared as one of the rules and was substantially attributed (mistakenly) to Pixar rather than Adams. The framework's appeal lies in its pedagogical clarity and its substantial alignment with classical narrative structure: 'Once upon a time' establishes setting and protagonist; 'Every day' establishes status quo and protagonist's normal life; 'One day' provides inciting incident disrupting the status quo; 'Because of that... Because of that' chains causal consequences (the rising action of three-act structure); 'Until finally' provides climactic resolution; 'And ever since then' establishes new equilibrium showing transformation. The framework has been substantially adopted in narrative-design education across film, animation, advertising, marketing, education, and substantial commercial storytelling-craft training. The Story Spine works well as introductory tool for understanding causal narrative structure and for developing story premises before substantial elaboration. Critics note that the framework's clean causal chain ('because of that... because of that') may oversimplify narrative structure — many successful narratives involve substantial parallel plot threads, ensemble structure, or causal complexity that the linear spine doesn't capture. The misattribution to Pixar (the framework predates Pixar's adoption and was developed by Adams) demonstrates the credit-attribution challenges in story-craft methodology.

name: Dramatica Theory
one_line_summary: Phillips and Huntley's framework treating story as an analogy for a single mind solving a problem.
extended_summary: Dramatica Theory is the elaborate narrative-theory framework articulated by Melanie Anne Phillips and Chris Huntley in their 1993 Dramatica: A New Theory of Story (substantially expanded over multiple editions through 2004), treating story as an analogy for a single mind solving a problem — with characters representing different facets of human psychology (logic, emotion, conscience, etc.) and dramatic structure mirroring cognitive-emotional problem-solving processes. The framework's central commitments include: (1) story as model of mental problem-solving; (2) eight 'character archetypes' (Protagonist, Antagonist, Reason, Emotion, Sidekick, Skeptic, Guardian, Contagonist) representing distinct narrative functions tied to mind functions; (3) four 'throughlines' simultaneously developing in story (Overall Story, Main Character, Impact Character, Subjective/Relationship); (4) extensive elaborated typology of story elements with substantial taxonomic specification (theme types, problem-solving styles, plot points, etc.); (5) the 'storyform' as specific configuration of choices that produces a particular story. Dramatica is substantially distinguished from other narrative frameworks by its theoretical ambition (providing comprehensive theory of all story rather than practical structural template) and its extensive taxonomic apparatus (substantially more elaborate than Three-Act Structure, Save the Cat, or other practical frameworks). The framework has substantial commercial implementation through Dramatica software (developed by Phillips, Huntley, and Stephen Greenfield) that allows writers to develop stories through the framework's elaborate choice-trees. Dramatica has substantial dedicated user community but limited mainstream Hollywood adoption — the framework's substantial complexity creates substantial learning curve, and many professional screenwriters find it more academic than practically useful. Critics including substantial story-craft commentators argue Dramatica's theoretical apparatus is genuinely demanding without producing better stories than simpler frameworks, that its 'mind analogy' framing is more metaphorical than substantively analytical, and that its commercial software promotes a specific framework over alternatives.

name: Polti's 36 Dramatic Situations
one_line_summary: Catalog of underlying dramatic conflicts found across all stories.
extended_summary: Polti's 36 Dramatic Situations is the catalog of underlying dramatic conflicts articulated by French writer Georges Polti in his 1895 Les Trente-Six Situations Dramatiques (translated as The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations 1916). Polti's foundational claim, citing earlier work by Carlo Gozzi and Goethe (Goethe reportedly told Schiller that Gozzi maintained 'there can be but thirty-six tragic situations' and Schiller, after working at the problem, concluded the same), was that all dramatic narratives can be analyzed into 36 fundamental conflict situations — combinations of moral elements creating dramatic tension that Polti claimed to have systematically catalogued through analysis of substantial body of dramatic literature. The 36 situations include: Supplication, Deliverance, Crime Pursued by Vengeance, Vengeance Taken for Kin Upon Kin, Pursuit, Disaster, Falling Prey to Cruelty/Misfortune, Revolt, Daring Enterprise, Abduction, The Enigma, Obtaining, Enmity of Kinsmen, Rivalry of Kinsmen, Murderous Adultery, Madness, Fatal Imprudence, Involuntary Crimes of Love, Slaying of a Kinsman Unrecognized, Self-Sacrificing for an Ideal, Self-Sacrifice for Kindred, All Sacrificed for a Passion, Necessity of Sacrificing Loved Ones, Rivalry of Superior and Inferior, Adultery, Crimes of Love, Discovery of the Dishonor of a Loved One, Obstacles to Love, An Enemy Loved, Ambition, Conflict with a God, Mistaken Jealousy, Erroneous Judgment, Remorse, Recovery of a Lost One, Loss of Loved Ones. Each situation specifies dramatic dynamic between roles (e.g., Persecutor and Persecuted in Supplication; Avenger and Criminal in Vengeance). The framework has been substantially influential in narrative analysis and creative writing education, providing analytical vocabulary for examining dramatic structure across genres and traditions. The 36-number specificity is substantially debated — Polti's enumeration involves substantial subjective categorization, and alternative dramatic-situation catalogs (Tobias's 20 Master Plots 1993, Booker's 7 Basic Plots 2004) provide substantively different enumerations. The framework's enduring appeal lies in its catalog form rather than its specific enumeration — the broader claim that recurring conflict patterns underlie diverse stories has substantial intuitive appeal even if the specific 36 are contested.

name: Vogeler's Writer's Journey
one_line_summary: Writer's adaptation of Campbell's monomyth for screenwriters.
extended_summary: Vogler's Writer's Journey (the manifest spelling 'Vogeler' is a typographical variant) is the practical screenwriting adaptation of Joseph Campbell's monomyth articulated by Christopher Vogler in his 1985 Disney memo 'A Practical Guide to The Hero with a Thousand Faces' (substantially circulated within Disney as story-development methodology) and elaborated in his 1992 book The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers (with substantial subsequent editions). Vogler's framework distills Campbell's elaborate seventeen-stage monomyth (departure, initiation, return) into twelve practical stages for screenwriters: (1) Ordinary World; (2) Call to Adventure; (3) Refusal of the Call; (4) Meeting the Mentor; (5) Crossing the First Threshold; (6) Tests, Allies, and Enemies; (7) Approach to the Inmost Cave; (8) Ordeal; (9) Reward; (10) The Road Back; (11) Resurrection; (12) Return with the Elixir. The framework substantially shaped Hollywood story development from the 1980s onward — Vogler's Disney memo is widely credited with influencing Disney's substantial narrative-success run including The Lion King, Beauty and the Beast, and the Disney Renaissance generally; subsequent screenwriting practice across studios has substantially adopted hero's-journey thinking. The framework's enduring appeal lies in its claim to articulate universal narrative pattern that explains why certain stories resonate deeply — a claim Campbell himself made about the monomyth as pattern underlying all human storytelling. Substantial scholarly critique has complicated these universality claims: Campbell's 'monomyth' has been argued to be substantially Western-androcentric, with substantial alternative frameworks proposed (Maureen Murdock's Heroine's Journey 1990 substantially critiquing Campbell's gendered framing; substantial folklore and anthropology critique that Campbell substantially overgeneralizes from selective evidence). The framework remains substantially influential in commercial Hollywood while facing substantial scholarly contestation about its universality claims.

name: Aristotle's Poetics
one_line_summary: Foundational analysis of tragedy with concepts of mimesis, catharsis, hamartia, peripeteia.
extended_summary: Aristotle's Poetics is the foundational text of Western literary and dramatic theory, written by Aristotle in the 4th century BCE (estimated 335 BCE), substantially analyzing the nature of poetry and dramatic literature with particular focus on tragedy. The text was substantially lost during late antiquity and rediscovered through Arabic preservation and translation in medieval period, with substantial Renaissance recovery shaping subsequent Western literary theory. Aristotle's foundational concepts include: (1) Mimesis — imitation or representation, with poetry as imitation of human action through different media (rhythm, language, harmony); (2) Tragedy as 'imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude... through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions' — the foundational tragic-effect theory; (3) Catharsis — the emotional purgation or clarification produced by tragedy, with substantial subsequent debate about whether catharsis means purgation (Freud-influenced reading), purification, or intellectual clarification; (4) Six elements of tragedy in order of importance: plot (mythos), character (ethos), thought (dianoia), diction (lexis), melody (melos), spectacle (opsis); (5) Hamartia — the tragic 'error' or 'flaw' of the protagonist (substantially debated whether this means moral flaw, error of judgment, or tragic mistake); (6) Peripeteia — reversal of fortune, often through unexpected discovery; (7) Anagnorisis — recognition or discovery, often producing peripeteia; (8) Unity of action — single coherent action with beginning, middle, end (subsequent Renaissance interpreters extended this to unities of time and place that Aristotle didn't substantially advocate); (9) Probable vs possible — well-constructed plots prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities. The Poetics has substantially shaped Western literary criticism for 2300+ years and remains foundational to contemporary dramatic theory, narrative studies, and creative writing education despite being a substantially incomplete text (only the section on tragedy survives; the section on comedy is famously lost).

core_components: Mimesis (imitation/representation); Tragedy definition emphasizing pity and fear; Catharsis (substantially debated meaning); Six elements: plot, character, thought, diction, melody, spectacle; Hamartia (tragic error/flaw); Peripeteia (reversal of fortune); Anagnorisis (recognition); Unity of action; Probable vs possible; Distinction between epic and tragedy; Foundation of Western literary theory; Substantial Renaissance recovery and reinterpretation; Lost comedy section; Substantial 2300+ year influence

common_criticisms: The Poetics is substantially incomplete — only the section on tragedy survives, with the famously lost section on comedy substantially limiting Aristotle's full theory of poetry; substantial interpretive disagreement about key concepts (catharsis meaning, hamartia meaning) has continued for 2300+ years without resolution; Aristotle's analysis substantially reflects the specific Greek tragic theater he knew (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides) — generalization to other dramatic traditions is contested; Renaissance interpreters (particularly Italian neoclassicists like Castelvetro) substantially extended Aristotle's analysis with substantial inventions (the unities of time and place that Aristotle didn't advocate) that subsequent dramatic practice has substantially complicated; cross-cultural application of Aristotelian framework has uneven results — non-Western dramatic traditions (Sanskrit drama, Chinese opera, Japanese Noh) have substantially different theoretical frameworks; tendency for Aristotelian analysis to substantially privilege tragedy over comedy and other dramatic forms; substantial 20th-century critique (Brecht's epic theater, theater of the absurd, postmodern theater) explicitly challenges Aristotelian dramatic principles; integration with contemporary narrative theory (cognitive narratology, affective response research) is incomplete; commercial educational use sometimes presents Aristotle as 'the' theory of drama without engaging substantial subsequent theoretical alternatives; the text's Greek-specific cultural assumptions about heroism, fate, and divine order shape commitments that don't always transfer.

name: Show Don't Tell
one_line_summary: Craft principle preferring scene and sensory detail over exposition.
extended_summary: Show Don't Tell is the foundational creative-writing principle preferring concrete dramatization (scene with sensory detail, action, dialogue) over abstract exposition (telling the reader what to think or feel). The principle's foundational articulation is typically attributed to Anton Chekhov's letter to his brother Alexander (1886): 'Don't tell me the moon is shining; show me the glint of light on broken glass' (the wording is substantially apocryphal — the actual Chekhov letter says something similar but the famous phrasing is later paraphrase) and to Henry James's substantial early-20th-century criticism arguing for dramatized presentation over narrative summary. The principle was substantially codified through 20th-century creative-writing pedagogy, particularly in the substantial American creative-writing program tradition that emerged from the Iowa Writers' Workshop (founded 1936) and proliferated globally. The principle's central commitment: rather than narrating that 'John was angry' (telling), show John's anger through his actions, words, expressions, and the sensory details of the scene (showing) — letting readers experience the emotion through dramatic presentation rather than receiving authorial assertion. Show Don't Tell substantially shapes contemporary creative writing across fiction, screenwriting, journalism, memoir, and increasingly business storytelling. Critics including substantial creative-writing teachers note that the principle is too absolute as commonly stated — many successful narratives benefit from substantial telling for pace, exposition, summary, stylistic effect, voice, and reader-narrator intimacy; the contemporary 'show don't tell' rule sometimes produces overwritten descriptive prose with limited narrative drive; experienced writers know when to show and when to tell, with the rigid rule sometimes producing mechanical writing in unsophisticated hands. Substantial recent creative-writing pedagogy has shifted toward 'show and tell' or context-dependent application of the principle.

name: In Medias Res
one_line_summary: Beginning a narrative in the middle of action rather than at the chronological start.
extended_summary: In Medias Res (Latin: 'into the middle of things') is the narrative technique of beginning a story in the middle of action rather than at chronological beginning, with backstory and prior events revealed subsequently through flashbacks, exposition, dialogue, or other narrative devices. The technique was articulated by Roman poet Horace in his Ars Poetica (c. 19 BCE), where he praised Homer for plunging into the middle of action ('in medias res non secus ac notas auditorem rapit') in the Iliad and Odyssey rather than starting at chronological beginning (with the Iliad starting in the ninth year of the Trojan War, the Odyssey starting with Telemachus seeking news of his absent father). The technique provides multiple narrative advantages: immediate engagement with action rather than slow setup; raises questions readers want answered (creating narrative tension through suspended exposition); allows distillation to the most dramatic and significant portion of the story rather than starting with less interesting earlier events; aligns with how memorable events are often experienced in real life — abruptly, without anticipatory framing. The technique substantially descends from epic-poetry tradition through medieval romance, Renaissance drama, novelistic tradition (substantial 19th-century novelistic adoption including Wuthering Heights with its disorienting frame structure), 20th-century modernist fiction (Faulkner, Conrad, others substantially using in medias res with substantial chronological complexity), and contemporary screenwriting and novel-writing practice. In medias res is substantially recommended in screenwriting and creative-writing pedagogy as antidote to slow openings — many writing-craft handbooks recommend starting in the middle of action rather than 'on a calm day before everything changed.' The technique works in tension with the requirement to provide enough context for readers to engage with the action — too much in medias res produces disorientation; too little produces conventional chronological openings.
